The life cycle of Mantidactylus grandidieri begins with the deposition of small, yolk-laden eggs into the still waters of Madagascar's eastern rainforest streams. Each egg weighs approximately 0.0042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0042 grams] upon oviposition, a modest initial mass that reflects the energetic constraints of producing gelatinous clutches in a nutrient-poor aquatic environment. The duration of the embryonic development period is tightly linked to water temperature. Under laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the interval between egg deposition and larval eclosion spans roughly 110 days after hatching , a comparatively prolonged incubation phase that may reduce predation risk for the developing embryos by extending the period during which they remain concealed within their protective jelly capsules.

Following eclosion, the free-swimming tadpoles of Mantidactylus grandidieri embark on an exotrophic feeding phase, grazing on periphyton and suspended organic particles. Larval growth proceeds steadily until the onset of metamorphosis, a critical developmental transition that marks the shift from an aquatic to a terrestrial existence. The snout-vent length at which this morphological transformation begins is notably small, with individuals typically measuring only 1.6 centimeters  at the start of metamorphic climax. This value places the species among the smaller-bodied metamorphs within the Mantidactylus genus, suggesting that early transition to land may be an adaptive response to the ephemeral nature of their breeding pools. The tail resorption and limb bud development that characterize this stage are completed over several weeks.

Post-metamorphic juveniles, or froglets, emerge onto the forest floor and begin a period of rapid somatic growth. This terrestrial juvenile phase is characterized by intensive foraging on small arthropods, allowing the young frogs to accumulate the body mass necessary for future reproductive effort. The attainment of sexual maturity, marked by the onset of gametogenesis and the appearance of secondary sexual characteristics in males, occurs when individuals reach a snout-vent length of 6 centimeters [Lp = 6 centimeters]. This size threshold appears to be a reliable indicator of physiological readiness, as it corresponds with the development of functional gonads and the ability to engage in amplexus. The growth trajectory from metamorphosis to puberty is heavily influenced by prey availability and local thermal regimes.

Once sexually mature, adult Mantidactylus grandidieri continue to grow, albeit at a decelerated rate, until they approach their maximum body size. The ultimate snout-vent length attained by fully grown individuals is 8 centimeters [Li = 8 centimeters], a dimension that places this species among the larger members of its genus. Corresponding to this skeletal size, the ultimate wet weight of a reproductively active adult is approximately 52.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 52.3 grams]. This asymptotic mass reflects the culmination of the species' lifetime growth trajectory and represents the optimal body size for balancing the energetic demands of maintenance, locomotion, and reproduction within the species' humid forest habitat. Field studies indicate that males and females reach comparable maximum sizes.

Reproductive output in Mantidactylus grandidieri is substantial, with females capable of producing multiple clutches across a single breeding season. Under the stable thermal conditions of 27 °C [T = 27 °C] that prevail in their lowland rainforest habitat, the maximum reproductive rate is realized when females lay approximately 22 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 22 eggs per clutch] and, by producing roughly 364 clutches per year [F_R_i = roughly 364 clutches per year], achieve an impressive total annual fecundity. Total lifespan under these same thermal conditions is considerable; the maximum longevity recorded for the species is 6 years [am = 6 years], a duration that allows for repeated breeding seasons and contributes to population persistence across variable environmental conditions at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C].
